title: In Catilinam I — Opening (§1-2)
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source_notes: Latin text from the Oxford Classical Text tradition (Clark). Translation by C. D. Yonge, 'The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero' (1856).
reading_notes: Cicero's First Catilinarian is the most famous piece of Latin oratory. Delivered in the Temple of Jupiter Stator to a full Senate with Catiline himself present, Cicero opens with the rhetorical hammer 'Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?' Every Latin student meets this sentence; it is the template of Ciceronian periodic style. Note the praeteritio, the ascending cola, the second-person address: Cicero weaponizes grammar.

lines.original: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
lines.english: How long, O Catiline, will you abuse our patience?
lines.gloss: Quo usque = 'up to what point, how long'; tandem = 'pray, at last' (intensifier); abutere = 'will you abuse' (2nd sg. future of abutor, deponent; + ablative object); Catilina = 'Catiline' (vocative); patientia nostra = 'our patience' (ablative object of abutere).

lines.original: Quam diu etiam furor iste tuus nos eludet?
lines.english: How long will that madness of yours still mock us?
lines.gloss: Quam diu = 'how long'; etiam = 'still, even'; furor iste tuus = 'that madness of yours' (iste is the demonstrative of contempt); nos = 'us' (accusative); eludet = 'will mock, elude' (3rd sg. future of eludo).

lines.original: Quem ad finem sese effrenata iactabit audacia?
lines.english: To what end will your unbridled audacity hurl itself?
lines.gloss: Quem ad finem = 'to what end'; sese = 'itself' (reflexive accusative); effrenata = 'unbridled' (nominative, agreeing with audacia); iactabit = 'will throw, hurl' (3rd sg. future of iacto); audacia = 'audacity, daring' (nominative subject).

lines.original: Nihilne te nocturnum praesidium Palati, nihil urbis vigiliae, nihil timor populi, nihil concursus bonorum omnium, nihil hic munitissimus habendi senatus locus, nihil horum ora vultusque moverunt?
lines.english: Do the nightly guards of the Palatine, the watches of the city, the fear of the people, the gathering of all good men, this most defended meeting-place of the senate, the faces and expressions of these men — none of this has moved you?
lines.gloss: Nihilne = 'nothing?' (nihil + interrogative ne, repeated for rhetorical effect); te = 'you' (accusative, object of moverunt); nocturnum praesidium Palati = 'nightly guard of the Palatine' (nominative, singular); urbis vigiliae = 'watches of the city' (nominative plural); timor populi = 'fear of the people'; concursus bonorum omnium = 'gathering of all good men'; hic ... habendi senatus locus = 'this place for holding the senate' (habendi is gerund genitive); horum ora vultusque = 'the faces and expressions of these (men)'; moverunt = 'have moved' (3rd pl. perfect of moveo).

lines.english: Do you not perceive that your plans lie open?
lines.gloss: Patere = 'to lie open, be exposed' (infinitive of pateo); tua consilia = 'your plans' (nominative, subject of infinitive); non sentis = 'do you not feel, perceive' (2nd sg. of sentio, + accusative-and-infinitive).

lines.original: Constrictam iam horum omnium scientia teneri coniurationem tuam non vides?
lines.english: Do you not see that your conspiracy is now held fast, bound by the knowledge of all these men?
lines.gloss: Constrictam = 'bound, constrained' (accusative, agreeing with coniurationem); iam = 'already'; horum omnium = 'of all these' (genitive plural); scientia = 'knowledge' (ablative of means); teneri = 'to be held' (passive infinitive of teneo); coniurationem tuam = 'your conspiracy' (accusative, subject of infinitive); non vides = 'do you not see' (2nd sg. of video).

lines.original: Quid proxima, quid superiore nocte egeris, ubi fueris, quos convocaveris, quid consili ceperis, quem nostrum ignorare arbitraris?
lines.english: What you did last night and the night before, where you were, whom you called together, what plan you took up — which of us do you think is ignorant of this?
lines.gloss: Quid = 'what'; proxima ... superiore nocte = 'last night, the night before' (ablative of time); egeris = 'you did' (2nd sg. perfect subjunctive of ago, indirect question); ubi fueris = 'where you were' (subjunctive); quos convocaveris = 'whom you called' (subjunctive of convoco); quid consili ceperis = 'what plan you took' (consili = partitive genitive); quem nostrum = 'which of us'; ignorare = 'to be ignorant' (infinitive); arbitraris = 'do you think' (2nd sg. deponent of arbitror).

lines.english: O the times! O the customs!
lines.gloss: O = 'O' (vocative interjection); tempora = 'times' (accusative plural, vocative of exclamation); mores = 'customs, morals' (accusative plural, vocative of exclamation). This is perhaps the single most famous Latin exclamation.

lines.original: Senatus haec intellegit; consul videt; hic tamen vivit.
lines.english: The Senate understands these things; the consul sees them; yet this man lives.
lines.gloss: Senatus = 'Senate' (nominative); haec = 'these things' (accusative plural neuter); intellegit = 'understands' (3rd sg.); consul = 'consul' (nominative); videt = 'sees'; hic = 'this man' (nominative, pointing at Catiline); tamen = 'yet'; vivit = 'lives'.

lines.original: Vivit? Immo vero etiam in senatum venit, fit publici consili particeps, notat et designat oculis ad caedem unum quemque nostrum.
lines.english: Lives? Nay, he even comes into the Senate, becomes a sharer of public counsel, and with his eyes marks out and designates each of us for slaughter.
lines.gloss: Vivit? = 'he lives?' (rhetorical question); Immo vero = 'nay rather, indeed' (strong correction); etiam = 'even'; in senatum venit = 'he comes into the senate'; fit = 'he becomes' (3rd sg. of fio); publici consili particeps = 'a sharer in public counsel' (nominative + genitive); notat = 'marks, notes'; designat = 'designates, picks out'; oculis = 'with his eyes' (ablative); ad caedem = 'for slaughter'; unum quemque nostrum = 'each one of us' (accusative, partitive genitive).
